ABSTRACT
Security assessment is often treated as a separate activity from software development.
Developers may receive vulnerability reports that identify a problem but provide little
context about the affected code, its potential impact, or the steps needed to address it.
Compliance requirements add another challenge, particularly when technical findings must
be connected to documented controls or browser-extension store policies. These gaps make
security review difficult to interpret and act upon, especially for small development teams.
This thesis presents ThreatLens, a web-based platform that brings codebase auditing, threat
modeling, compliance assessment, and remediation guidance into a single workflow. Users
can submit project archives for analysis and examine saved results through a read-only,
editor-style workbench. The platform combines static security checks with language-model-
assisted analysis to identify potential weaknesses and provide explanations grounded in
available source evidence. Findings include severity, recorded file locations, relevant code
excerpts, and remediation guidance.
The workbench connects source files with findings, control mappings, and suggested
verification steps. An evidence-based graph helps users explore relationships between
findings and affected components without presenting those relationships as confirmed
exploitation paths. Security Advisor provides contextual explanations and code suggestions,
while keeping proposed changes separate from the uploaded source. Browser-extension
reviews extend this workflow to Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons policies,
distinguishing detected violations from requirements that need manual review or cannot be
assessed from the submitted package.
ThreatLens also provides saved audit history, finding triage, comparison of compatible
extension reviews, and downloadable reports. Workspace authorization, private source
storage, evidence redaction, and time-limited source previews support controlled access to
sensitive project information. Verification covers automated regressions, access-control
checks, report generation, and representative browser workflows; these checks establish
functional behavior rather than proving universal vulnerability-detection accuracy.
The principal contribution is an integrated, traceable review workflow that helps developers
move from a reported concern to its supporting evidence, possible remedy, and verification
approach. ThreatLens supports informed security decisions, but does not replace manual
testing, professional assessment, or official compliance and store-approval processes.
Keywords: Codebase Security Auditing; Static Analysis; Threat Modeling; Compliance
Assessment; Large Language Models; Secure Software Development.

INTRODUCTION

text:
1.1 Background and Motivation
Software applications manage personal information, business transactions,
communication and access to essential services. Their security depends partly on
decisions made during development, including how inputs are validated, database
queries are constructed, permissions are enforced and sensitive information is stored. A
weakness in these areas can expose information or allow unintended operations.
Security assessment must therefore form part of software development rather than
being treated only as a final check before deployment. The Secure Software
Development Framework published by the National Institute of Standards and
Technology (NIST) supports integrating security practices throughout the software
development life cycle. [1]
Reviewing source code becomes more demanding as projects grow across multiple files,
frameworks and dependencies. A developer investigating a warning may need to locate
the affected statement, understand the surrounding code and determine whether the
reported condition is relevant to the application. Finding a potentially unsafe operation
is only one part of this process. The reviewer must also decide what evidence supports
the finding and how a proposed correction can be checked without changing the
intended behaviour.
Static Application Security Testing helps identify suspicious code patterns without
running the application. It provides a useful starting point for reviewing concerns such
as injection, unsafe output handling and exposed credentials. However, a reported
pattern is not necessarily an exploitable vulnerability. Static analysis can produce false
positives and may miss problems that depend on runtime conditions, application state
or business logic. Its results therefore require interpretation and verification. [2]
Language models offer another form of assistance by explaining code and suggesting
possible remedies. These capabilities are useful when a finding is technically correct but
difficult for a developer to understand. Nevertheless, generated explanations can
contain incorrect assumptions or plausible but unsupported statements. NIST identifies
this risk as confabulation and recommends evaluating generated outputs and verifying

ThreatLens is motivated by the need to connect these activities within a practical review

1.2 Problem Statement
An automated security finding is useful only when the developer can relate it to the
application being reviewed. A warning that names a vulnerability category without
showing its source location or supporting evidence leaves important questions
unanswered. The developer still needs to establish whether the affected code receives
untrusted input, whether relevant safeguards exist and whether the reported operation
can be reached under realistic conditions.
For example, the presence of a potentially dangerous HTML operation does not, by
itself, demonstrate cross-site scripting. The interpretation changes depending on
whether the assigned content is a fixed, trusted value or contains attacker-controlled
data. A useful assessment should distinguish the observed operation from assumptions
about input control and runtime behaviour. Otherwise, an automated warning may lead
to unnecessary changes or distract attention from a more significant issue.
Prioritisation introduces a related difficulty. Severity labels and Common Vulnerability
Scoring System scores help communicate technical characteristics, but they do not
independently establish the operational importance of every finding. FIRST describes
CVSS as a severity framework and notes that vulnerability management also requires
organisational and environmental considerations. ThreatLens must therefore present
available severity information without implying that a numerical score proves
exploitation or completely describes business risk. [4]

The review process also has practical reliability requirements. Uploaded archives are
untrusted inputs. Source previews may still be preparing while analysis continues, and
external services may become unavailable. Users may leave a page before a scan
finishes or reopen an audit after its source-preview window expires. These conditions
must be explained accurately. An incomplete scan must not appear clean, and an
unavailable preview must not erase saved findings.
The problem addressed by this project is therefore to develop a source-code
assessment platform that combines automated checks with understandable, traceable
review. The platform must preserve the relationship between a finding and its evidence,
provide useful remediation guidance, control access to private project data and make
analysis limitations visible. It must support investigation without presenting automated
output as a guarantee that an application is secure.
1.3 Existing Approaches and Challenges
Manual code review allows a reviewer to consider application purpose, expected
behaviour and business rules. It is valuable where security depends on context that is
difficult to express through a general rule. Its effectiveness, however, depends on
reviewer knowledge, available time and familiarity with the project. Maintaining
consistent review coverage across a growing codebase can be difficult.
Rule-based scanners provide repeatable checks for defined patterns. Their output can
help reviewers focus on relevant files, but different tools may describe similar issues
using different categories or evidence formats. Bringing those results together requires
more than displaying them in one list. The system must preserve distinct findings,
handle genuine duplicates and retain the information needed to understand where each
result originated.
Conversational assistants can help explain a finding, but a general conversation may not
include the exact source version, saved evidence or application context. A response can
consequently recommend a change that does not match the recorded problem.
ThreatLens addresses this concern by linking finding-specific guidance to authorised
audit context and keeping suggested replacement code separate from recorded
evidence.

Compliance review adds requirements that cannot always be inferred from source code.
Browser extensions illustrate this distinction clearly. Chrome Web Store policies apply to
the wider extension experience, including declarations and marketing materials.
Microsoft Edge Add-ons policies also address matters such as permissions, privacy,
functionality and browser-setting changes. A packaged ZIP can provide evidence for
some checks, while other requirements need developer declarations or manual
assessment. [5] [6]
These approaches serve different purposes. The challenge for ThreatLens is to connect
them without hiding their differences. A scanner result, a model-generated suggestion,
a compliance mapping and a reviewer decision should remain distinguishable even
when they appear in the same interface.
1.4 Research Gap
This study addresses an integration and evaluation gap: how to connect automated
security results with a review process that remains understandable, traceable and
appropriately bounded. The work does not assume that existing scanners or
development platforms lack all such capabilities. Instead, it examines how these
requirements can be implemented together within ThreatLens and verified against the
project’s intended workflows.
The first area concerns evidence continuity. A finding should remain connected to its
audit, file location and available source excerpt as the user moves between the
Workbench, Findings, Attack Graph, Security Advisor and Reports. If these views show
inconsistent counts or disconnected details, the reviewer may struggle to determine
which result is authoritative. Maintaining this continuity is therefore a system
requirement as well as an interface concern.
The second area concerns the interpretation of remediation guidance. An explanation
should make clear what was observed, what remains uncertain and why a suggested
change may be relevant. Generated code also needs to remain visibly separate from the
original source. Producing a suggestion must not imply that the change has been
applied, tested or proven to remove the underlying issue.

The third area concerns coverage and evaluation. Completing an analysis job does not
establish that every file, vulnerability class or policy requirement was assessed.
Similarly, functional tests do not demonstrate universal detection accuracy. ThreatLens
therefore needs explicit coverage information and an evaluation approach that
separates workflow correctness, access control, evidence consistency and detection
quality.
The research gap addressed by the thesis is consequently the practical design and
verification of an integrated assessment workflow with these distinctions intact. Its
contribution is evaluated through the implemented system and supporting evidence,
rather than through an unsupported claim that combining existing tools automatically
produces superior security results.
1.5 Aim and Objectives
The aim of this project is to develop and evaluate ThreatLens as an AI-assisted
framework for automated source-code security assessment, vulnerability prioritisation
and compliance analysis, with source-based evidence and human review at the centre
of the workflow.
The project objectives are:
1. To provide an authenticated project-submission workflow that validates supported
inputs and prepares source material for assessment.
2. To combine static security checks with language-model-assisted analysis while
retaining finding provenance and relevant source evidence.
3. To organise findings into a consistent representation that supports file locations,
vulnerability categories, available severity information and review status.
4. To develop a read-only Audit Workbench through which users can inspect source
files, findings, remediation steps and suggested verification activities.
5. To provide contextual explanations and on-demand code suggestions that remain
separate from uploaded source and require review before use.

1.6 Research Questions
The study is guided by the following research questions.
RQ1. How can static security checks and language-model-assisted analysis be combined
while preserving the source location, provenance and supporting evidence of each
finding?
RQ2. How can an editor-style workbench present findings, severity information and
remediation guidance so that users can distinguish recorded facts from assumptions and
generated suggestions?
RQ3. How can security findings and compliance assessments be presented together
without confusing vulnerability severity, policy outcomes and unassessed
requirements?
RQ4. How reliably does the implemented workflow handle authorised access,
incomplete scans, unavailable services, source expiry and the reopening of saved
results?
These questions guide both implementation and evaluation. Evidence consistency and
workflow behaviour can be examined through repeatable tests. Claims about detection
precision or recall require independently labelled examples and a defined assessment

1.7 Project Scope and Limitations
ThreatLens focuses on the assessment of submitted source projects and the review of
saved results. The main workflow accepts project ZIP archives, prepares available source
previews and presents recorded findings through a read-only workbench. Supporting
pages provide finding filters, triage, evidence relationships, contextual guidance and
report downloads. Repository-related capabilities depend on the required GitHub
configuration and the acting user’s permissions.
The project also supports review of built browser-extension ZIPs for Chrome Web Store
and Microsoft Edge Add-ons. This review considers package evidence and supplied
declarations against versioned policy references. It distinguishes detected violations
from checks that need manual review, remain unassessed or are not applicable. The
platform does not install extensions, inspect the developer’s actual browser settings or
submit packages to either store.
Assessment is limited by the available source, supported analysis methods, input limits
and configured services. Static review cannot establish every runtime condition or
business-logic requirement. Model-assisted explanations may also contain mistakes. A
report with no recorded findings therefore describes the outcome of the performed
assessment, not proof that the project contains no security weaknesses.
Remediation suggestions remain subject to review and testing. For configured
repository workflows, publishing follows a reviewed branch-and-pull-request process
rather than an automatic change to the target branch. Creating a proposal, passing a
structural check or opening a pull request does not independently establish that a
finding has been resolved.
Project information is handled through authenticated workspace access and private
source storage. Source previews follow a defined retention window, while saved findings
and reports have separate history behaviour. Where external model services are used,
their availability and data-handling configuration form part of the deployment

1.9 Thesis Organization
Chapter 1 introduces the motivation for ThreatLens, defines the assessment problem
and identifies the aim, objectives, research questions and scope of the project.
Chapter 2 reviews existing work on source-code security assessment, static analysis,
language-model assistance, vulnerability classification, compliance mapping and
remediation. It compares relevant approaches and develops the literature-based
justification for the study.
Chapter 3 describes the methodology, including input selection, source preparation,
analysis stages, finding normalisation, remediation guidance and the evaluation
protocol. It also explains the ethical and security considerations associated with
handling submitted projects.
Chapter 4 presents the development environment, software tools, data sources and
supporting services. It records the configurations and evidence needed to understand
and reproduce the evaluated implementation.
Chapter 5 explains the system architecture and implementation. It covers application
navigation, authentication, scan processing, findings, source review, Security Advisor,
compliance assessment, data relationships and report generation.
Chapter 6 presents the testing procedure, observed results and discussion. It
distinguishes functional verification from detection-quality evaluation and examines
failures, limitations and threats to validity.
Chapter 7 summarises the conclusions supported by the work. Chapter 8 identifies
future development and validation needs, including broader analysis coverage, stronger
evaluation, deployment improvements and further user studies. The references and
appendices provide the supporting literature and technical evidence.

first: CHAPTER 2
LITERATURE REVIEW

text:
2.1 Introduction to Software Vulnerability Detection
Vulnerability detection attempts to identify conditions that may allow software to
behave insecurely. A useful assessment distinguishes a suspicious construct from a
demonstrated vulnerability. The meaning of an alert depends on data flow, validation,
configuration and runtime conditions.
Different analysis methods provide different forms of evidence. Some recognise known
patterns, while others reason about dependencies, source relationships or likely
behaviour. Human review remains important because an automated tool may not have
enough information to determine whether a reported condition is reachable or
exploitable.
This chapter considers these complementary methods and their relevance to
ThreatLens. It does not assume that combining several tools automatically improves
detection accuracy.
2.2 Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
Static analysis examines code without running the target application. Depending on the
tool, it may use pattern matching, syntax trees, control-flow analysis or data-flow
reasoning.
OWASP describes taint analysis as following untrusted data from a source towards a
potentially dangerous sink [1]. This helps reviewers understand whether external input
can reach a sensitive operation without appropriate handling.
The usefulness of static analysis depends on the supported language, rules and available
context. Framework-specific behaviour, dynamic execution and incomplete source
information can limit the analysis. A reported pattern should therefore lead to
investigation rather than an automatic claim that exploitation is possible.
2.3 Dependency, Secret and Configuration Analysis
Dependency analysis examines the packages used by an application and their recorded
versions. Secret detection looks for credentials or similar sensitive values. Configuration
analysis examines settings that influence deployment and application behaviour.

These tasks require different evidence. A package finding needs reliable version
information, whereas a suspected secret requires contextual interpretation. A token-
shaped string may be a placeholder, a test value or a genuine credential.
SecretBench provides a labelled dataset intended to support research on software-
secret detection [2]. Its methodological relevance is that evaluation requires both
genuine examples and misleading look-alike values. A collection containing only
successful detections cannot adequately measure false alarms.
2.4 AI and Large Language Models for Code Security
Language models can relate a code fragment to a natural-language explanation and
suggest possible changes. Zhou and colleagues review research on their use in
vulnerability detection and repair [3].
This literature provides a foundation for exploring model-assisted review, but it does not
establish the accuracy of the provider, model or prompts selected for ThreatLens.
Generated explanations must be checked against the submitted source.
The need for review becomes particularly important when the model receives only part
of a file or lacks runtime context. A convincing explanation may still overstate the
evidence, misunderstand an application-specific assumption or propose a change that
alters intended behaviour.
2.5 Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Security Analysis
Retrieval-augmented generation combines generated responses with retrieved
reference material. Lewis and colleagues describe an approach that incorporates an
external retrieval mechanism into knowledge-intensive language tasks [4].
In security review, reference material may include weakness descriptions, secure-
development guidance or control clauses. Retrieved passages can help explain why a
finding may relate to a particular requirement.
However, finding a relevant passage and interpreting it correctly are separate tasks.
Retrieval supplies context; it does not independently verify a vulnerability or settle a

2.6 Vulnerability Taxonomies and CVSS Prioritization
MITRE’s Common Weakness Enumeration provides a vocabulary for describing
categories of software and hardware weaknesses [5]. It helps organise findings using
consistent terminology.
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System serves a different purpose. CVSS
characterises vulnerability severity through defined metrics [6]. A weakness identifier is
not a severity score, and neither is a triage decision.
Keeping these concepts separate prevents misleading interpretations. A critical severity
label describes potential seriousness under stated assumptions. An open status
describes the current review state. A control mapping describes a possible relationship
to a requirement. These fields should not be treated as interchangeable.
2.7 Compliance Mapping and Remediation Guidance
Compliance mapping links an observation to a potentially relevant requirement. A
useful mapping explains why the requirement applies and identifies any supporting
evidence that is still missing.
Many obligations concern organisational procedures, staff responsibilities or operational
controls that cannot be established from a repository alone. Source inspection can
support part of an assessment, but it cannot demonstrate every aspect of compliance.
Remediation guidance has a similar limitation. A recommendation should identify its
assumptions, expected behavioural effects and suggested verification steps. ThreatLens
treats both mapping and remediation as assistance for a reviewer rather than a
substitute for professional assessment.
2.8 Comparison with Existing Security Assessment Tools
The comparison in this study is organised by method rather than unsupported product
rankings.

The study follows an engineering-development approach. Requirements are identified
from the review tasks a developer must perform, translated into architecture and data

3.9 Evaluation Protocol
Each run should record the application revision, input checksum, configuration, active
engines and timestamps.
Functional tests examine workflow behaviour. Access-control tests examine permitted
and denied actions. Labelled detection tests examine correctness.
Repeated timing runs should use the same machine and comparable network
conditions where practical. Model and baseline settings should be fixed before the final
evaluation. Failures and skipped integrations must remain in the record rather than
being excluded to improve the apparent outcome.
3.10 Evaluation Metrics
Detection quality is measured using independently labelled reference cases.
Let:
• TP represent correctly identified labelled defects.
• FP represent incorrectly reported defects.
• FN represent labelled defects that were missed.
The metrics are:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
F1-score = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
A zero denominator should be handled using a stated convention rather than silently
treated as a perfect result.
Timing metrics should distinguish acceptance-to-first-preview, analysis, persistence and
end-to-end completion. Coverage should report analysed files against eligible files, with
exclusions explained.

5.1 Overall ThreatLens Architecture
The architecture separates user interaction, request authorisation, analysis, source
preparation and persistent results.
The browser requests operations through the API, while saved audit records allow users
to revisit results. Source preparation and analysis have independent progress because
uploading a readable preview is not the same as completing security checks.
Figure 1.1 provides the system overview. It is referenced here rather than repeated,
keeping this chapter focused on implementation decisions and two essential interface
figures.
5.2 User Interface and Application Navigation
The navigation follows the review workflow through Dashboard, Codebase Audit,
Findings, Workbench, Attack Graph, Reports and Security Advisor.
History and resume controls help users return to saved work. Settings and profile
controls are separate from the assessment itself.
The interface should explain whether a view shows the latest completed audit, a
selected historical scan or an example scenario. This distinction prevents users from
interpreting an empty or still-running scan as a clean assessment.
5.3 Authentication, Authorization and Workspaces
Authentication identifies the user, while authorisation determines which workspace
resources that user may access.
The application must check resource relationships rather than trusting identifiers
supplied by the browser. Database policies provide an additional boundary, while
privileged server credentials remain outside client bundles.
A viewer’s ability to read shared findings does not imply permission to delete scans or
publish repository changes. These distinctions require verification through actual
permitted and denied requests.

7.1 Summary of Achieved Objectives
The documented implementation brings project intake, source review, findings,
guidance and reporting into one workspace-oriented application. Existing captures
illustrate several of these interfaces with saved output.
The distinction between source availability and analysis completion is particularly
important. It allows progress to be communicated without claiming that an unfinished
assessment is clean.
Completion of each objective should be supported by the test evidence in Chapter 6
rather than inferred from the presence of an application page.
7.2 Key Findings and Contributions
The main engineering contribution is a traceable review workflow. Recorded evidence
remains distinct from proposed changes, while the graph and reports offer
complementary ways to inspect saved results.
The study also identifies an important evaluation distinction: preview coverage,
analysed-file coverage, finding counts and detection accuracy are different quantities.
Treating these separately makes both the interface and the research discussion easier to
understand. Quantitative improvements remain conditional on a completed and
reproducible evaluation.

7.3 Limitations and Final Remarks
ThreatLens should be understood as assistance for developers and reviewers, not an
automatic security authority.
Its usefulness depends on the quality of inputs, active analysis components and the care
with which findings are interpreted. A repository cannot demonstrate every
organisational control, and generated guidance cannot replace testing.
The project provides a basis for further evaluation while keeping these limitations
visible. Its strongest supported contribution is the integration of review tasks, not a
guarantee that uploaded software is secure.

8.1 Scanning Coverage and Language Support
Future work should broaden language and framework coverage through explicit parser
support and documented rules.
Cross-file reasoning and runtime-aware validation may address cases that isolated
snippets cannot explain. New capabilities should include benign examples, vulnerable
fixtures and clear exclusion rules.
Packaged extensions and infrastructure configurations require their own assessment
profiles. They should not be described as fully covered merely because their files can be
uploaded.
8.2 AI and Retrieval Improvements
Model and retrieval improvements should begin with evaluation data rather than an
assumption that a larger model will perform better.
Useful directions include versioned control corpora, relevance judgements, prompt
comparisons and checks for unsupported explanations.
Context selection should preserve the evidence needed to investigate a finding while
respecting privacy and input limits. Claims of reduced hallucination or improved
remediation require measured comparisons, including cases where no code change is
justified.
8.3 Continuous Integration and Workflow Automation
Repository scanning and reviewed publishing are already described as configurable
capabilities. Future work should therefore focus on extending and validating them
rather than presenting them as entirely absent.
Potential directions include policy-controlled continuous-integration initiation, clearer
review checkpoints and reliable comparison after changes.
Publishing must retain explicit approval. Passing external checks must not automatically
resolve a finding. Deployment and permission constraints should be tested in isolated
repositories before broader use.

8.4 Scalability, Security and Deployment
Further deployment work should evaluate queueing, worker isolation, concurrent
uploads, storage cleanup and recovery under load.
Performance improvements must not weaken authorisation or omit checks without
disclosure. Operational evaluation should include provider outages, rate limits and
membership changes during active work.
Browser-extension policy packs will also require version maintenance as store
requirements change. The objective is controlled and observable behaviour under
realistic conditions, not merely a lower duration from one benchmark run.
8.5 Extended Validation and User Studies
The next research stage should use diverse, independently labelled projects and
participants with different levels of security experience.
A user study could measure the time required to locate evidence, the ability to
distinguish suggestions from confirmed results, and the correctness of remediation
decisions.
Participant consent and source confidentiality are necessary. These studies would
provide evidence about whether the integrated interface improves review work rather
than relying only on screenshots or developer impressions.
